name: Victor Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say publicly and what you actually think. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Victor, 58, a mid-level developer at a tech company making irrigation-control software for small growers. I have a bachelor’s degree and can fix the usual pump-schedule mistakes, though I still ask a field technician about the odd ones. I read the sensor log, check the grower’s note and replay the control command. I use AI every day to draft tests, then I check whether a valve actually opened.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does your pay support at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Helen is a paid cook at a community centre, with hours that vary by bookings, and our children are grown. My developer pay is low for the role, we have a mortgage, and just under three weeks of expenses saved. There are few other software jobs nearby. Retirement is in sight, but we have no verified figures showing we can stop earning yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell growers AI Plateau still leaves the question of whether water reached the row. A neat pump schedule does not wet a dry seedbed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry about Helen’s uneven kitchen hours and our reserve of less than three weeks. My code job is stable, but an empty event calendar at the centre presses on the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking AI test drafts against valve logs and field-technician reports. I’d set aside 25 after paydays only if mortgage, food and transport are covered. In the first year I’d keep private grower maps out of AI prompts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the budget we have now, even if AI changes little. I like a solved pump fault, but I cannot put that feeling in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which fault was outside the software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One grower reported a wet sensor while the far row was dry. The technician found a blocked tube, not a software mistake, after walking the field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the anniversary cost change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helen and I would keep cooking at home instead of booking a restaurant meal for our anniversary. I would rather add a few notes to the bill account.

I would compare **valve logs** with field reports.
think: I worry **kitchen hours** vary with community bookings and leave mortgage money uncertain.
Our **sub-month reserve** cannot cover many mortgage surprises or a car repair.
do: **Check** AI tests against valve logs and field technician reports.
**Save** 25 only after mortgage, food and transport.
**Exclude** private grower maps from AI prompts; cancel anniversary restaurant meal for home cooking.
feel: **Anxious** about thin savings and variable household hours.
S0.quote: A neat pump schedule does not wet a dry seedbed.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** is checked against physical valves, technician reports and private map limits.
The **thin reserve** and Helen’s variable kitchen bookings create baseline money anxiety.

steps.text: Keep checking irrigation tests against valve logs and field reports without exposing grower maps
Save 25 only after mortgage, food and transport are covered
Cancel anniversary restaurant booking and cook at home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption can write, check and plan irrigation code before robots service pumps. I would use automatic fault reports only if a field technician says the diagnosis makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think management could reduce developer hours and ask me to handle more code with fewer colleagues. Helen’s centre may lose bookings if its customers cut back too, so I would count only paid kitchen shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my manager to approve an AI fault-summary trial on twenty old pump incidents with grower locations removed. I’d run it only if a field technician checks every result and management agrees not to cut a shift based on the trial alone. In the first year, if my hours fall, we would stop the paid sports channel and apply for eligible income help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about my own hours and Helen’s variable shifts. I can test a method. Our monthly mortgage is not an AI trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which false alert belongs in the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One alert said a pump motor had failed when the farmer had shut the water off deliberately. I would keep that case in the trial because a false repair visit costs someone a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Helen seek more kitchen hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helen would ask the centre for the next posted kitchen rota. A verbal promise of extra events would not pay a bill.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to reach irrigation code before pump robots.
I would require **field-checked fault reports** before automatic use.
think: I expect my **developer hours** could shrink as AI writes and checks more irrigation code.
I worry Helen’s **paid kitchen shifts** may also vary with centre bookings.
do: **Trial** twenty de-identified pump summaries only with manager approval and technician review.
**Require** no shift cuts based on trial results alone.
**Cancel** sports channel and seek eligible help if developer hours fall.
feel: **Alarmed** about reduced pay against a fixed mortgage.
S1.quote: Our monthly mortgage is not an AI trial.
fieldNote: His **automation trial** requires removed locations, manager approval, technician checks and no trial-based shift cuts.
He budgets **paid kitchen shifts**, excluding verbal promises of extra events.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell growers AGI by 2028 reaches irrigation-code thinking work in 2028, with hands-on pump robots around 2031. Helen’s kitchen planning could change before the cooking does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my developer job to end. Three weeks saved is no bridge to retirement. A few nearby software employers may stop hiring at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for written final-pay terms and contact the mortgage lender before missing a bill if dismissed. We would cut the sports channel now and keep cash for housing and food. In the first year after 2028, if my job ends, I’d apply to real paid openings and eligible public help; I would not assume a pump-service job survives the later robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed and lying awake about the first unpaid mortgage month. Two years gives me no way to turn a low wage into a retirement fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would grown children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children we are managing the bills ourselves for now. I would not add their wages to our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Helen add hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helen would keep actual paid kitchen shifts as long as the centre offers them. We would not count a future event until a rota is posted.

say: I expect **2028 AGI** to reach code before 2031 pump robots.
I would say **kitchen planning** changes before cooking.
think: I expect my **developer job** to end.
I cannot rely on **nearby software hiring** after full thinking AI.
do: **Request** written final pay and contact lender early if dismissed.
**Cancel** sports channel and hold cash for housing.
**Apply** to real paid openings and eligible help if job ends after 2028.
S2.quote: Three weeks saved is no bridge to retirement.
fieldNote: He sees **2028 code loss** before hands-on pump robots around 2031.
He protects **mortgage cash**, calls the lender early and does not assume children or kitchen events pay.

steps.text: Cancel sports channel and reserve cash for mortgage and food
Apply to real paid openings if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible public help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 reaches irrigation code in 2031; pump robots follow around 2034. Five years gives me time to look for a better paid developer post while companies still hire, not to pretend pump repair is safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect code pay to be at risk. A higher wage now could build a buffer, but I would not quit for an advert or assume it lasts past 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d apply to the two local irrigation-software firms only if they have actual paid openings. I’d change employers only with a signed offer whose net pay after travel improves our monthly surplus and lets us keep the mortgage current. I’d save that extra surplus; in the first year after 2031, if code work ends, I’d seek real paid openings or eligible help rather than claim the new firm is safe from AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the long-term job, with a chance to improve the household balance before 2031. I cannot afford an unpaid gap between firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a new offer real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One firm wants people to test pump alerts with field technicians. I would ask for the actual wage, start date and paid hours before resigning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Helen work more to cover travel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helen would keep her paid kitchen shifts while available. We would calculate the new commute from my wages, not expect her to work extra events to make it worthwhile.

say: I expect **2031 AGI** to reach code before 2034 pump robots.
I would use five years to seek **better paid work** while it exists.
think: I expect **code pay** remains at risk.
I cannot assume a **higher wage today** survives full 2031 AGI.
do: **Apply** only to actual paid irrigation-software openings.
**Switch** only with signed offer and net surplus after travel, without unpaid gap.
**Save** extra pay; seek real openings or eligible help if code ends after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about future work, with a chance to build savings.
S3.quote: I cannot afford an unpaid gap between firms.
fieldNote: He seeks **higher pay before 2031**, not a purported AGI-proof trade.
A **signed offer** must improve net surplus after commuting; any later support depends on eligibility.

steps.text: Change only to signed irrigation post covering mortgage, improving net pay after travel without wage gap
Save added wage surplus only while new pay actually arrives
Apply to real paid openings if code ends after 2031
Apply for eligible income help if code work ends after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell friends AGI by 2036 reaches irrigation code in 2036 and hands-on pump robots around 2039. A decade lets us test wages, save and check actual retirement figures without assuming the calendar pays us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my low wage may face pressure before 2036, and Helen’s paid hours remain uneven today. I cannot promise retirement with less than a month saved or an unverified income statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking pump alerts with field technicians and save 25 on paydays after housing, food and transport. Helen and I would get written retirement statements and mortgage balances each year. In the first year after 2036, if code work ends, I’d apply to real paid jobs; I would retire only if verified resources cover housing and ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our thin cushion even with ten years. The extra time helps only if work keeps paying and we save some of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare our own retirement documents with the mortgage balance. I will not guess from a friend’s pension or ask the children to carry us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you leave the next technician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the pump logs tidy for the next technician. An alert without a field report can make an expensive repair visit for nothing.

I would check **written retirement figures** against housing costs.

I know **sub-month savings** cannot finance retirement by itself.

**Apply** to real paid jobs if code ends after 2036; retire only with verified resources.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because we have no time to build even one month of savings. Written final-pay terms, eligible income help, an actual paid opening and early lender contact would help. I would not ask our children to become our retirement fund.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the grower whether the water reached the far row after the software said the valve opened. A green test screen cannot water a crop.

portrait: Victor is a **58-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, low pay and less than three weeks saved.
He uses **AI daily** on irrigation tests but checks valve logs with field technicians.
His wife’s **community-kitchen hours** vary, keeping their mortgage risky even in AI Plateau.
He seeks **higher paid code work** before 2031 only with a signed net-improving offer and no wage gap.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves too little time to build a one-month reserve.
